lesson.text: Quick memory: what is a chorus? (The part of a song with the same words and tune every time.) Today: writing a song of your own.
A song's words are its lyrics. Each syllable usually gets its own note: but-ter-fly has 3 syllables, so it needs 3 notes.
Put strong syllables on strong beats. Say ba-NA-na: the middle syllable is strong. Sing it so NA lands on a strong beat, and the word sounds natural.
Rhymes make lines fit together and easy to remember: night and light, day and play. They usually come at the ends of lines.
The chorus is the heart of a song: short, catchy and repeated. Many songwriters write it first. Its hook is the catchiest bit, a few words and notes that stick in your head.
Worked example: 'Sun is shin-ing, time to play' has 7 syllables, so it needs 7 notes. Ending on the home note, C, makes it sound finished.
Repeat and change: sing a line, repeat it, then change its end. Steps make a tune easy to sing; a leap on an important word makes it stand out.
Try it in the world: write a 4-line chorus about your favourite place in your world. Rhyme the ends of lines 2 and 4. Clap its syllables, then sing it. Next: great composers.

exercises.prompt: How many syllables does the word dinosaur have?
exercises.hint: Clap the word as you say it slowly.
exercises.explain: di-no-saur: 3 syllables, so it needs 3 notes.

exercises.prompt: In most songs, each syllable gets its own note.
exercises.explain: True: one note for each syllable is the usual way to fit words to a tune.

exercises.hint: Say each word after play. Which ends with the same sound?
exercises.explain: Play and day end with the same sound: they rhyme.

exercises.prompt: Listen. How many notes did you hear?
exercises.hint: Count each new sound, on your fingers.
exercises.explain: C, D, E and C: 4 notes.

exercises.prompt: A song line goes: We sail across the sea. One note for each syllable: how many notes does it need?
exercises.hint: Clap it slowly. Long words have more than one clap.
exercises.explain: we sail a-cross the sea: 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6 notes.

exercises.prompt: In ba-NA-na, which syllable should land on a strong beat?
exercises.hint: Say the word. Which syllable do you say most strongly?
exercises.explain: We say ba-NA-na with the middle syllable strong, so NA goes on the strong beat.

exercises.prompt: Listen to the claps for butter-fly, butter-fly, then mark the boxes.
exercises.hint: Butter is two quick claps; fly is one longer one.
exercises.explain: You heard ti-ti, ta, ti-ti, ta: claps in boxes 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7.

exercises.prompt: Which note is best to end a song in C major on, so it sounds finished?
exercises.hint: Which note feels like home in C major?
exercises.explain: C is the home note of C major, so ending on it sounds finished.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of writing a song in order.
exercises.hint: Many songwriters start with the chorus.
items: Fit the words to a tune
Choose what the song is about
Sing it, and change what doesn't fit
exercises.explain: Choose a topic, write the chorus, then the verses, fit them to a tune, and sing it to improve it.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.explain: Lyrics are the words, the hook the catchiest bit, a syllable one beat of a word, and a rhyme ends the same.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Which line fits this tune, one note for each syllable?
exercises.hint: Count the notes, then count each line's syllables.
choices: Sun is shining, time to play
The sun is shining brightly in the sky
exercises.explain: The tune has 7 notes, and Sun is shin-ing, time to play has 7 syllables.

exercises.prompt: Listen to the claps for wa-ter-mel-on, then mark the boxes.
exercises.hint: Four quick claps, one for each syllable.
exercises.explain: The claps are in boxes 1, 2, 3 and 4.

exercises.prompt: Listen to the claps of a song line. How many syllables does it have, one clap each?
exercises.explain: 5 claps, so the line has 5 syllables.

exercises.hint: Look at the last word of each line.
choices: The stars are bright / They shine all night
The stars are bright / They shine all day
I like the sea / I like the sky
We run and play / We sing a song
exercises.explain: Bright and night end with the same sound, so those lines rhyme.

exercises.prompt: A hook is a short, catchy part of a song that sticks in your head.
exercises.hint: Think of the chorus's catchiest bit.
exercises.explain: True: the hook is the part you can't stop humming.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Which words fit this tune, one note for each syllable?
exercises.explain: The tune has 5 notes, and Hel-lo, my good friend has 5 syllables.
